title: Influences of mental accounting on consumption decisions: asymmetric effect of a scarcity mindset
authors: Cheng, L.; Yu, Y.; Wang, Y.; Zheng, L.
tldr: Scarcity mindset moderates mental accounting effects on consumption, reducing hedonic preference under windfall gains but not affecting hard-earned money decisions.
problem_and_motivation: Mental accounting influences consumer behavior but may vary across populations and contexts. A scarcity mindset may alter how consumers operate their mental budgets, potentially moderating the effects of mental accounting on consumption decisions.
approach: Two-sample experimental design with college students (n=319) and adults (n=294).
2x2 between-subjects design manipulating mental account (windfall vs hard-earned) and consumption type (hedonic vs utilitarian).
Scarcity mindset measured using 3-item Likert scale (Cronbach's alpha 0.83-0.88).
Chi-square tests and logistic regression models analyzed consumption preferences.
Online experiment conducted via survey platforms in China.
findings: num: Windfall gains lead to hedonic consumption preference (chi-square=33.45, Cohen's d=0.68, p<0.001 for students).
num: Hard-earned money leads to utilitarian consumption preference (chi-square=10.30, Cohen's d=0.38, p=0.001 for adults).
num: Scarcity mindset reduces hedonic consumption under windfall condition (B=-0.66, SE=0.30, p=0.026 for students).
num: Scarcity mindset moderates windfall effects on consumption (B=-1.28, SE=0.30, p<0.001 for adults).
Scarcity mindset does not significantly affect consumption under hard-earned money condition.
Adult consumers prefer utilitarian consumption regardless of mental account type.
Students show stronger hedonic preference under windfall gains than adults.
Asymmetric effect of scarcity mindset across different mental accounts demonstrated.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: The study demonstrates that scarcity mindset asymmetrically moderates mental accounting effects on consumption decisions. It shows that windfall gains lead to hedonic consumption, but this effect is reduced under high scarcity mindset. Hard-earned money consistently leads to utilitarian consumption regardless of scarcity levels. The research provides evidence for the mindsponge theory in explaining consumption behaviors across different psychological states.

limits: Scarcity mindset measured using self-reported scale rather than experimental manipulation.
Study conducted only in China, limiting cross-cultural generalizability.
Gain amounts differed between student and adult samples, potentially affecting results.
Psychological mechanisms underlying scarcity mindset effects remain unexplored.

Domains 3.A (Expense Categorization Frameworks) and 3.C (User-Defined Allocation Constraints) assigned contextual relevance as paper discusses mental accounting and money categorization. All other domains (1-2, 4-14) rejected as paper focuses on consumer psychology and behavioral economics rather than personal finance systems, demographic profiles, or technical components.

limitations: Scarcity mindset measured using self-reported scale rather than experimental manipulation.
Study conducted only in China, limiting cross-cultural generalizability.
Gain amounts differed between student and adult samples (100 vs 3000 yuan).
Psychological mechanisms underlying scarcity mindset effects remain unexplored.
No demographic variables included as covariates beyond age and gender.
